severity.summary: SATS level 2 (emergency, seen within 10 minutes). A 38-year-old woman with advanced HIV (CD4 9) has had 6 weeks of failed empirical TB treatment. She now has fever, new confusion, pancytopenia, AKI (eGFR 30), hyponatraemia (124), relative hypotension (BP 95/59, MAP 71) and ferritin 18000. qSOFA is 3/3 and HLH-2004 criteria are met (5/8, 3 not assessable). HScore is 222-321 against a cut-off of 169. This pattern suggests secondary HLH triggered by a disseminated opportunistic infection or malignancy, with multi-organ involvement and possible adrenal insufficiency. Circulatory failure cannot be formally judged because lactate and vasopressor data are missing. MAP is above 65, so it is not documented. Her risk is high because deterioration is likely without urgent action, not because circulatory collapse is established. She needs a monitored resuscitation bay, senior review and a time-critical diagnostic and treatment plan.
redFlags: New confusion in a patient with CD4 9: exclude cryptococcal or TB meningitis, other CNS infection, and metabolic causes (hyponatraemia, uraemia, hypoglycaemia)
qSOFA 3/3 with fever, BP 95/59 and AKI: possible sepsis with evolving organ dysfunction
Pancytopenia with ferritin 18000 and fever: HLH criteria met
Hypotension with sodium 124: adrenal insufficiency (TB, fungal or CMV adrenalitis) must be considered

Failure of 6 weeks of RHZE with negative GeneXpert and TB-LAM: TB not excluded, but a second or different opportunistic infection is likely (disseminated histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, NTM/MAC, CMV, lymphoma)
New skin papules: may be disseminated fungal infection (cryptococcus, histoplasma), disseminated TB, Kaposi sarcoma or a drug eruption; skin biopsy gives rapid tissue diagnosis
eGFR 30: affects drug choice (amphotericin formulation, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, cotrimoxazole, tenofovir)
Pregnancy status not stated: must be established, because cytopenias, AKI and confusion would otherwise raise HELLP, TTP and other pregnancy-related diagnoses

leadingDiagnosis.name: Secondary (infection-associated) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in advanced HIV, with the trigger most likely a disseminated opportunistic infection (disseminated TB that is partially treated or drug-resistant, disseminated histoplasmosis or cryptococcosis), with lymphoma still to be excluded
leadingDiagnosis.rationale: HLH-2004 is met (5/8) and HScore is 222-321. Supporting findings are fever, pancytopenia, ferritin 18000 and CD4 9. The cause remains uncertain: TB (negative Xpert and LAM do not exclude it), disseminated fungal disease (skin papules, confusion, pancytopenia, CD4 below 100), NTM/MAC or CMV (CD4 below 50), and lymphoma. HLH is secondary until proven otherwise, so the aim is to find and treat the trigger while HLH-directed therapy is decided with haematology. The probability is moderate because HLH-2004 is not yet fully assessable (triglycerides, fibrinogen, sCD25, marrow and spleen not done). Several alternative triggers remain plausible, and some of these (e.g. disseminated TB or fungal sepsis alone with hyperferritinaemia) could account for the picture without true HLH.

differential.name: Disseminated TB (paucibacillary, drug-resistant, or inadequately treated), possibly with adrenal involvement
evidenceFor: Fever, pancytopenia and very high ferritin are compatible with disseminated TB
Negative Xpert and LAM do not exclude TB in advanced HIV
Microbiology taken after weeks of treatment may be falsely negative
Hypotension with hyponatraemia is compatible with adrenal TB
evidenceAgainst: No improvement after 6 weeks of RHZE (suggests resistance, malabsorption, non-adherence, or a different or additional diagnosis)
Negative GeneXpert and TB-LAM (limited negative predictive value)

differential.name: Disseminated histoplasmosis
evidenceFor: Fever with failure of TB treatment
Hypotension with hyponatraemia (adrenal involvement is possible)
Disseminated disease can mimic TB and trigger HLH
evidenceAgainst: No fungal testing has been done

differential.name: Cryptococcal disease (meningitis or disseminated)
evidenceFor: A negative TB workup does not explain the confusion
evidenceAgainst: CrAg and CSF not yet reported

differential.name: Lymphoma or other malignancy (HIV-associated lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma) as HLH trigger
evidenceFor: Lack of response to TB treatment
evidenceAgainst: No documented lymphadenopathy, mass or B symptoms beyond fever

differential.name: Disseminated MAC/NTM or CMV disease
evidenceAgainst: No cultures, PCR or imaging yet

differential.name: Adrenal insufficiency (TB, fungal or CMV adrenalitis) contributing to hypotension and hyponatraemia
evidenceFor: Advanced HIV with infections that infiltrate the adrenals
evidenceAgainst: Hyponatraemia has other plausible causes (SIADH from CNS or lung disease, hypovolaemia)

differential.name: Drug reaction (DRESS or severe cutaneous adverse reaction to RHZE or cotrimoxazole)
evidenceFor: Fever, skin lesions and cytopenias 6 weeks into new drugs
evidenceAgainst: Skin papules rather than a diffuse rash

differential.name: Bacterial sepsis or Pneumocystis pneumonia as co-infection
evidenceAgainst: No respiratory symptoms, hypoxia or focus documented

differential.name: Pregnancy-related thrombotic microangiopathy or HELLP, or TTP/HUS (to exclude if she is pregnant or recently postpartum; TMA also possible in advanced HIV)
evidenceFor: Cytopenia, AKI and confusion would fit if she is pregnant or recently postpartum
HIV is a TTP risk factor
evidenceAgainst: Pancytopenia (not isolated thrombocytopenia and anaemia) is less typical
No blood film or haemolysis markers yet

mustNotMiss.name: Cryptococcal meningitis
mustNotMiss.why: Confusion with CD4 9 is cryptococcal meningitis until excluded. The result changes ART timing and treatment, and raised intracranial pressure needs therapeutic drainage. A negative serum CrAg does not exclude it (prozone effect).
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: Serum CrAg now. Lumbar puncture with opening pressure and CSF CrAg, India ink/culture, cell count, protein and glucose. Do CT brain first only if there are focal signs, papilloedema or markedly reduced consciousness.

mustNotMiss.name: TB meningitis and disseminated TB (including drug-resistant TB)
mustNotMiss.why: TB remains possible despite negative Xpert and LAM, because the tests are insensitive and she has been on treatment for 6 weeks. Stopping treatment would be dangerous, and drug-resistant TB would need a regimen change.
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: CSF Xpert Ultra and culture. Blood mycobacterial culture. Xpert, LPA and culture on any specimen (sputum, urine, marrow, node, skin). Repeat urine LAM. Bone marrow and skin biopsy for AFB. Check adherence and absorption.

mustNotMiss.name: Disseminated histoplasmosis and other endemic or opportunistic fungal infection
mustNotMiss.why: It mimics TB, causes HLH and pancytopenia, and is rapidly fatal if untreated. It needs amphotericin-based therapy, not anti-TB drugs.
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: Urine and serum Histoplasma antigen if available. Fungal blood culture. Skin biopsy with GMS/PAS and fungal culture. Marrow histology and culture. Peripheral/buffy coat smear. If testing is unavailable and the patient is deteriorating, discuss empirical liposomal amphotericin B with ID/microbiology.

mustNotMiss.name: Adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis
mustNotMiss.why: Hypotension with hyponatraemia, fever and confusion in advanced HIV. It is treatable and life-threatening.
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: Random cortisol (before steroids), electrolytes including potassium, glucose. Give empirical IV hydrocortisone if she remains hypotensive or cortisol is low. Adrenal imaging (ultrasound or CT).

mustNotMiss.name: HIV-associated lymphoma / malignancy as the HLH trigger
mustNotMiss.why: HLH needs a trigger search; lymphoma is a treatable cause that will not respond to anti-infective therapy.
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine, skin or lymph node biopsy, CT or ultrasound for nodes and organomegaly, LDH.

mustNotMiss.name: Bacterial sepsis (including bacteraemia, Salmonella)
mustNotMiss.why: qSOFA 3/3 in an immunosuppressed host; delayed antibiotics increase mortality.
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: Blood cultures before antibiotics (without delaying them), lactate, urine culture, chest X-ray; start empirical IV antibiotics.

mustNotMiss.name: Pregnancy-related emergencies (HELLP, acute fatty liver) and TTP/HUS
mustNotMiss.why: Pregnancy status is not documented. Cytopenia, AKI and confusion with normal or low BP would be an obstetric emergency if she is pregnant or postpartum.
mustNotMiss.howToExclude: Urgent pregnancy test. If positive, urgent obstetric review. Blood film for schistocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, platelets, LFTs and coagulation.

bedsideStat.rationale: Confusion; exclude hypoglycaemia, which is common in sepsis and adrenal insufficiency.

bedsideStat.test: Full vitals including GCS, temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, repeat BP and urine output
bedsideStat.rationale: Establish a baseline and detect progression of circulatory compromise; qSOFA is 3/3.

bedsideStat.test: Venous or arterial blood gas with lactate
bedsideStat.rationale: Lactate is a missing input needed to judge the degree of circulatory dysfunction and tissue hypoperfusion in suspected sepsis; the Sepsis-3 shock criteria cannot be assessed without it.

bedsideStat.test: Point-of-care electrolytes (sodium, potassium), urea and creatinine
bedsideStat.rationale: Sodium 124 and eGFR 30; hyperkalaemia and low sodium with hypotension would support adrenal insufficiency.

bedsideStat.test: Random serum cortisol (draw before any steroid)
bedsideStat.rationale: Hypotension with hyponatraemia; adrenal insufficiency must be evaluated.
CD4 9 with confusion; a rapid test that guides LP and antifungal therapy. A negative result does not rule out disease if the load is very high (prozone effect).
Woman aged 38; pregnancy status not stated and affects differential, imaging and drug choices.

bedsideStat.test: Malaria rapid test or smear if travel to Limpopo/KwaZulu-Natal low-lying areas
bedsideStat.rationale: Fever and confusion; malaria is rapidly treatable and must not be missed.
Electrolyte and renal derangement; urine protein, blood and infection.

bedsideStat.test: Skin lesion examination, and smear or scraping from a papule for stain/microscopy
bedsideStat.rationale: Rapid clue to cryptococcus, histoplasma or AFB; also documents the lesions before biopsy.

first24h.test: Full blood count with differential, peripheral blood smear (schistocytes, parasites, intracellular yeasts on buffy coat), reticulocytes
first24h.rationale: Quantify pancytopenia; exclude TMA; look for yeast or haemophagocytes.

first24h.test: Blood cultures (bacterial) before antibiotics, plus blood culture for mycobacteria and for fungi
first24h.rationale: Sepsis, Salmonella, disseminated TB/MAC and fungaemia; mycobacterial blood culture has the best yield in CD4 below 50.

first24h.test: Lumbar puncture: opening pressure, CSF cell count, protein, glucose, CrAg, India ink, Gram stain, bacterial/fungal/mycobacterial culture, Xpert Ultra, VDRL or syphilis tests, ± CMV/VZV/HSV PCR
first24h.rationale: New confusion with CD4 9; needed to decide ART timing and treat meningitis. Do CT first only if focal signs, seizures, papilloedema or marked depression of consciousness; do not delay antibiotics or antifungals for imaging.

first24h.test: Liver function tests, LDH, triglycerides, fibrinogen, coagulation profile (INR/aPTT), D-dimer
first24h.rationale: HLH-2004 criteria not yet assessable (triglycerides, fibrinogen); hepatotoxicity from RHZE; DIC screen.

first24h.test: Soluble CD25 (sIL-2R), if available; repeat ferritin
first24h.rationale: Completes HLH-2004; trending ferritin follows response.

first24h.test: Urine lipoarabinomannan repeated; urine Histoplasma antigen and serum Histoplasma antigen where available
first24h.rationale: TB-LAM negative at presentation does not exclude TB; LAM is repeated for completeness; Histoplasma antigen is the key test for a fungal mimic.

first24h.test: Sputum (or induced sputum) for Xpert Ultra with rifampicin resistance and culture; urine and any other available specimen for Xpert/culture
first24h.rationale: Drug-resistant TB has to be considered since there has been no response.

first24h.test: Chest X-ray; ultrasound of abdomen (spleen, liver, nodes, adrenals, kidneys); CT chest/abdomen if available and renal function allows
first24h.rationale: Organomegaly (HLH criterion, HScore), lymphadenopathy, adrenal enlargement, hydronephrosis in AKI. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude TB or PJP.

first24h.test: CMV PCR (blood), EBV PCR, syphilis serology, hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody, HIV viral load
first24h.rationale: HLH triggers; HBV status guides ART regimen, particularly with renal impairment.

first24h.test: Urea/electrolytes, serum osmolality, urine sodium and osmolality, urine protein/creatinine ratio, urine microscopy
first24h.rationale: Characterise hyponatraemia (adrenal, SIADH, hypovolaemia) and AKI (pre-renal, ATN, drug-induced, infiltrative, TMA).

first24h.test: Differential count for eosinophils; haemolysis markers (haptoglobin, direct antiglobulin test)
Review adherence and drug history (directly observed treatment, vomiting, diarrhoea, concurrent medications)
first24h.rationale: Non-adherence or malabsorption could explain treatment failure.

definitive.test: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine: haemophagocytosis, cytology, histology (granulomas, lymphoma, fungal stains, AFB), plus culture for mycobacteria and fungi and Xpert
definitive.rationale: Confirms HLH features and finds the trigger (infection or malignancy); highest-yield single procedure for pancytopenia in advanced HIV.

definitive.test: Skin punch biopsy of a papule: histology with H&E, GMS/PAS and Ziehl-Neelsen stains, tissue culture (fungal and mycobacterial) and Xpert
definitive.rationale: Gives rapid tissue diagnosis of cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, TB, NTM, Kaposi sarcoma or drug eruption.

definitive.test: Lymph node or other lesional biopsy if lymphadenopathy or mass is found on imaging
Mycobacterial culture with drug susceptibility testing and line probe assay on positive cultures
definitive.rationale: Confirms or excludes drug-resistant TB or NTM.

immediate.action: Move to a monitored resuscitation or high-care bay. Secure IV access, continuous monitoring, hourly vitals, GCS and urine output.
immediate.rationale: SATS level 2 with qSOFA 3/3, confusion and possible evolving circulatory compromise.

immediate.action: Check bedside glucose immediately and correct if low.
Take blood cultures (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal) and lactate, then give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour without delaying for cultures or LP.
immediate.rationale: Suspected sepsis in a profoundly immunosuppressed host; delayed antibiotics increase mortality.

immediate.action: Give cautious IV isotonic (balanced) crystalloid titrated to perfusion with frequent reassessment; start vasopressors and escalate to ICU if hypotension persists after fluids.
immediate.rationale: BP 95/59 with AKI; avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid overload, and avoid rapid correction of sodium.

immediate.action: Draw random cortisol, then give empirical IV hydrocortisone if she remains hypotensive, if potassium is raised or glucose is low, or if cortisol is low or equivocal. Do not delay for the result if she deteriorates.
immediate.rationale: Hypotension with hyponatraemia raises adrenal insufficiency, a treatable cause of circulatory failure in advanced HIV; replacement is not the same as HLH-directed immunosuppression.

immediate.action: Perform lumbar puncture promptly (after CT only if focal signs, papilloedema or markedly reduced consciousness). Measure opening pressure and drain therapeutically if raised.
immediate.rationale: Confusion with CD4 9; cryptococcal and TB meningitis change management and ART timing.

immediate.action: Establish pregnancy status urgently; if pregnant or postpartum, request urgent obstetric review.
immediate.rationale: Changes differential (HELLP/AFLP/TMA) and drug and imaging choices.

targeted.action: Continue RHZE pending TB work-up, with pharmacist review for renal impairment (particularly ethambutol and pyrazinamide) and monitoring of liver function. Add pyridoxine if not already given.
targeted.rationale: TB is not excluded: Xpert and LAM have limited sensitivity at CD4 9, and cultures after 6 weeks of therapy may be falsely negative. Stopping would risk untreated TB.

targeted.action: Discuss empirical liposomal amphotericin B IV with ID or microbiology as soon as CrAg, CSF results and Histoplasma antigen are known, or earlier if she deteriorates before results. Prefer the liposomal formulation given eGFR 30. If CSF CrAg is positive, treat as cryptococcal meningitis per guideline (amphotericin-based induction with flucytosine, renal and marrow toxicity monitored).
targeted.rationale: Disseminated histoplasmosis and cryptococcosis are leading alternatives and are fatal without amphotericin. Pre-emptive treatment is justified if she is deteriorating and testing is delayed.

targeted.action: Urgent haematology discussion/referral for HLH (HLH-2004 5/8, HScore above cut-off), including marrow findings and the decision on HLH-directed therapy.
targeted.rationale: Secondary HLH in HIV is managed by treating the trigger; steroids or etoposide are given only with haematology and ID agreement once infection is covered, because immunosuppression can worsen uncontrolled infection.

targeted.action: Trigger search: do the investigations listed (marrow, skin biopsy, blood and CSF cultures, antigens, PCRs, imaging) in parallel rather than sequentially.
targeted.rationale: HLH is secondary until proven otherwise; infection (TB, fungal, MAC, CMV, EBV), lymphoma and drugs are possible triggers.

targeted.action: Consider empirical treatment for disseminated MAC or CMV, or PJP treatment, only if supported by results (CT chest, PCRs, culture, CD4 below 50 with a compatible picture) after ID discussion.
targeted.rationale: Avoids unfocused polypharmacy while keeping reversible causes in view.

targeted.action: Assess hyponatraemia: serum and urine osmolality, urine sodium, volume status, cortisol. Correct cautiously and avoid rapid rises in sodium.
targeted.rationale: Sodium 124 with confusion; risk of osmotic demyelination with overcorrection.

targeted.action: Review all nephrotoxic and renally cleared drugs. Avoid NSAIDs, contrast if possible, and tenofovir DF-containing ART at current eGFR. Seek nephrology advice if AKI progresses.
Plan ART according to timingDecisions after the LP, once meningitis is excluded or treated.
targeted.rationale: Early ART is life-saving at CD4 9, but timing depends on CNS findings and HLH trigger treatment.

supportive.action: Strict fluid balance, urinary output monitoring and daily electrolytes and renal function.
Transfuse blood products only against clinical thresholds or bleeding. Check coagulation and fibrinogen before any biopsy or LP.
supportive.rationale: Pancytopenia and possible HLH coagulopathy; biopsies and LP need haemostatic safety.

supportive.action: Airborne infection control precautions until TB is excluded or she has had adequate treatment; neuro observations and seizure and falls precautions.
Nutritional assessment and support, mouth care and screening for oral or oesophageal candidiasis.
supportive.rationale: Advanced HIV disease; malnutrition is common.

supportive.action: Identify next of kin and capacity; HIV counselling and adherence support; discuss goals of care with the family early given the high risk.
supportive.rationale: High mortality with HLH and advanced HIV; confusion limits consent.

existingTreatmentDecisions.reason: TB is not excluded. Negative GeneXpert and TB-LAM do not rule it out in CD4 9, and any test after 6 weeks of therapy can be falsely negative. Continue while the work-up for drug-resistant TB, NTM, fungal disease and lymphoma proceeds. Stop or modify only if there is: (a) a confirmed alternative diagnosis that explains everything, with TB excluded on adequate specimens including marrow and culture; (b) rifampicin resistance or other resistance on testing; (c) severe hepatotoxicity or drug hypersensitivity/DRESS. Ask the pharmacist to review renally cleared components (ethambutol, pyrazinamide) at eGFR 30, and check adherence and absorption.

timingDecisions.recommendation: Do not start ART today before the lumbar puncture and CSF results (CrAg, TB) are available. If cryptococcal and TB meningitis are excluded and she is stabilised on infection-directed therapy with HLH-directed treatment decided by haematology and ID, start ART early, within days to about 2 weeks. She is already 6 weeks into TB treatment, so ART is overdue unless a CNS infection is found. If cryptococcal meningitis is confirmed, defer ART for about 4-6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy. If TB meningitis is confirmed, delay ART per guideline (verify the interval) with specialist input. If there is disseminated histoplasmosis or another non-CNS infection, start ART early once she is clinically stable on antifungal treatment.
timingDecisions.reason: At CD4 9, early ART improves survival, but starting during active cryptococcal or TB meningitis increases mortality from IRIS in a closed space. Regimen choice needs renal and haematological adjustment: avoid tenofovir DF at eGFR 30 pending specialist advice, avoid zidovudine with pancytopenia, check HBV status, and adjust dolutegravir dosing for concurrent rifampicin using the pharmacy table. Monitor for IRIS after ART starts.

timingDecisions.recommendation: Perform as soon as she is stable and coagulation and platelets are known; do it before CT if there are no focal signs, papilloedema or markedly reduced consciousness.
timingDecisions.reason: Results determine antifungal therapy and ART timing; lack of CSF data is the main barrier to deciding on ART.

timingDecisions.recommendation: Defer until haematology and ID review, with infection-directed therapy started first. If she deteriorates rapidly, discuss with haematology the same day.
timingDecisions.reason: Immunosuppression before the trigger is treated can worsen disseminated infection. Marrow, cultures and antigens may change management within 24-72 hours.

timingDecisions.recommendation: Draw cortisol first. Give IV hydrocortisone if hypotension persists, potassium is raised, glucose is low, or cortisol is low or equivocal; do not delay if she deteriorates haemodynamically.
timingDecisions.reason: Hypotension with hyponatraemia; adrenal crisis is rapidly fatal and treatable.

timingDecisions.recommendation: Decide within hours with ID/microbiology once CrAg, Histoplasma antigen and CSF are back; start earlier if she worsens and results are delayed.
timingDecisions.reason: Disseminated histoplasmosis or cryptococcosis would otherwise remain untreated.

prophylaxis.indication: Indicated at CD4 below 200 (PJP, toxoplasma and bacterial prophylaxis). Check whether she is already taking it. Start or continue once she is stable, with adjustment for eGFR 30 by pharmacy and monitoring of blood counts, since pancytopenia and AKI are present and cotrimoxazole is a possible cause of drug reaction. If PJP is suspected or confirmed, treatment-dose therapy replaces prophylaxis.

Pre-emptive therapy is indicated if serum CrAg is positive and meningitis is excluded. If CSF CrAg is positive, treat as cryptococcal meningitis instead. It is not indicated as prophylaxis while the CrAg result is pending.
Not applicable: she is already on full TB treatment.
Not indicated if ART is started promptly; reconsider if disseminated MAC is excluded and ART is delayed, per guideline.

escalateIf: MAP below 65 mmHg, raised lactate, or a vasopressor requirement (documented circulatory failure): ICU referral
GCS falls, seizures, focal deficit or signs of raised intracranial pressure
Persistent hypotension or hyperkalaemia, or hypoglycaemia (adrenal crisis)
Rising creatinine, oliguria, severe acidosis or hyperkalaemia: nephrology and renal replacement discussion
Falling platelets or fibrinogen, bleeding, or DIC
Worsening hypoxia (PJP, ARDS, or HLH lung involvement)
Sodium falls below 120 or neurological features of hyponatraemia, or overly rapid correction
redFlags: No response to 6 weeks of RHZE
referral: Infectious diseases/internal medicine/HIV specialist (opportunistic infections, ART timing, antifungal therapy)
ICU or high-care review if circulatory failure is documented
Dermatology for biopsy support if needed
Obstetrics urgently if pregnant or recently postpartum
Clinical pharmacist for renal dose adjustments and drug interactions

questionAnswers.question: Should we continue TB treatment?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes, continue RHZE for now. Negative GeneXpert and TB-LAM do not exclude TB at CD4 9, and cultures taken after 6 weeks of treatment may be falsely negative. Non-response means the differential must widen: drug-resistant TB, non-adherence or malabsorption, NTM/MAC, disseminated histoplasmosis or cryptococcosis, CMV, lymphoma, and secondary HLH. Collect additional specimens (blood mycobacterial culture, marrow, skin and CSF with Xpert and culture, repeat urine LAM, sputum for resistance testing) and review renally cleared drugs with pharmacy. Reassess after results: stop or change TB treatment only if TB is convincingly excluded, resistance is shown, or there is serious drug toxicity or hypersensitivity.

questionAnswers.question: When should ART be started?
questionAnswers.answer: Not before the LP and CSF results. Cryptococcal or TB meningitis must be excluded first, because early ART in those conditions raises mortality. If meningitis is excluded and she is stabilised on infection-directed therapy with haematology input, start ART early, within days to about 2 weeks. She is already 6 weeks into TB treatment, so delay is not justified without a CNS reason. If cryptococcal meningitis is found, defer ART for about 4-6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy. If TB meningitis is found, delay per guideline with specialist input. Choose the regimen with renal function (avoid tenofovir DF at eGFR 30), pancytopenia (avoid zidovudine), HBV status and rifampicin interactions in mind, and monitor for IRIS.

uncertaintyFlags: The cause of the HLH-like picture is unknown; TB, histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, MAC, CMV, lymphoma and drug reaction all remain plausible, so no single trigger has a high probability.
HLH-2004 shows 5/8 with 3 criteria not assessable (e.g. triglycerides, fibrinogen, sCD25, marrow, spleen); HScore is missing organomegaly, fibrinogen, AST and marrow findings.
Circulatory failure cannot be judged: lactate and vasopressor data are missing. MAP is 71, so it is not documented.
Pregnancy status is not stated and could change the differential and management.
CrAg, CSF, Histoplasma antigen, cortisol, potassium, glucose, LFTs, platelet count, blood film and imaging are not reported.
Medication history is incomplete: adherence, cotrimoxazole use, previous ART exposure and other drugs are not stated; HBV status and viral load are unknown.
Exposure and travel history (endemic fungi, malaria areas) is not supplied.
The transfer question is for a draft to be checked by a reviewing doctor; the information given is insufficient for definitive decisions, so requiresDoctorReview = true.
